drills.title: vs Mohamed_Behery (840) — Queens Pawn Opening Horwitz Defense
drills.coachNote: You were already crushing, so grabbing the pawn on h7 wasn't the crime — missing the fork was. Nd5+ hits the king on e7 and the queen on c7 in one move; Black's forced exd5, then Rfe1+ drives the king to d6, and Qxf8+ wins the whole rook before it even gets to c6. Nxh7 only bags a pawn, and the game continues Rd8, Qf6+ Ke8, gxf4 — still winning, but you left a full rook on the board. Whenever you're this far ahead, look for the check that forks two pieces before you settle for a free pawn.

drills.title: vs edekyihotmailcom (766) — Queens Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: White's king on e2 has almost no squares left, which is your cue to hunt for mate, not a pawn. Nf4+ is a check the king can't block, so it's forced to e3, and Bc5# finishes it — the bishop covers e3 while the king's own pieces seal every escape. Qxe5+ only wins a pawn, and it hands White a way out: Ne4 blocks the check, and after Bxe4, Qc1, O-O-O the king runs to safety and the mate is gone. When the enemy king is stuck in the center with nowhere to go, always check for forced mate before grabbing material.

drills.title: vs edekyihotmailcom (766) — Queens Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: White's king is still stuck on e1 and the e5 pawn is undefended, so this was a moment to check first, not retreat. Qg3+ forces Ke2, then Qxe5+ grabs that pawn with check too — Kf2, Qd4+, Ke2 — you pick up material on every move while the king keeps getting shoved around. Ne6 instead pulls back a piece that wasn't even attacked, and White gets a free tempo to regroup with Qc1. The knight retreat isn't wrong forever, it's just too early — you had forcing checks on the board first. When the enemy king can't castle, always look for the check before you play the quiet move.

drills.coachNote: Both d4 and f4 defend the knight on e5, so trading into it with Nxe5 is only an even swap — and not even a good one. After fxe5, that pawn now attacks your knight on f6, forcing Nd7 next move, and White gets a strong protected pawn on e5 plus a free tempo to build with Ne2 and c5. Compare that to Nxd4: the pawn on d4 is defended only by the queen on d1, so that one's a clean, free pawn, and after Ne2 chases you, the knight just hops safely to f5. Before trading, scan for the piece that's actually only defended once — that's the one you take.

drills.coachNote: The g4 square sits right on White's queen's diagonal — d1, e2, f3, g4 are all open — so jumping the knight there just hands it over: Qxg4 wins it clean, since nothing of yours guards g4 yet. That's the whole story behind the big swing here. e5 first is the fix: it challenges the center, and only after dxe5 does Ng4 actually work, because the position's changed enough that White answers with Nf3 instead of just grabbing the knight. Before hopping a piece onto a square that looks empty, trace the diagonal or file behind it — a queen with a clear lane across the board is exactly what's easy to miss.

drills.coachNote: You were basically winning outright here — up a queen's worth of material — so the job was not to lose the thread. Bd6 looks natural, but it takes your own rook off the d-file, and once your queen wanders to a4, Black gets real play with Rb6 and then Rd8, hitting your rook on d2 with nothing backing it up — your advantage drops from nearly +20 to a merely-good +5. Rd7 was cleaner: double your rook onto the seventh immediately, before Black can organize any of that, trading down into a completely won position after Rd6, Bxd6. When your opponent has a pawn one step from promoting, that's the only thing that matters until it's dealt with.

Play Bd7 instead and that bishop stays alive on c6, so White just grabs it a second time with Bxd7+, Qxd7 — trading off your other bishop too, except now White never paid for the first capture, so you're down a full piece for nothing. Rad8 skips that chance and lets White dictate instead: Bh6 comes with tempo, g6 is forced to deal with it, and only then does White swap on e6 with Bxe6 fxe6 - the same trade happens a move later, but now your kingside pawns are weakened, over a pawn worse than it needed to be. Even after Qd6 saves the queen, Nxd8 still grabs the rook, and Qxd8 Qxg5 mops up a pawn too, keeping your advantage enormous. Qg5 ignores that entirely, and even though you're still completely winning on paper, it hands Black's queen and rook time to come after your own king - Rxf2 Qe5 Rf3 Rf1 shows them crashing into your position with real threats, exactly the kind of moment that let this game slip away later despite the huge material edge. When you're up this much, actively hunt for the move that finishes the game rather than one that merely maintains the lead - the opponent only needs one swindle.

drills.explanation: Qxc8 wins the rook on c8 outright — Black never dares recapture, since your bishop on f6 and rook on e7 strangle his king; he tries Qb5, and after Re8 he must throw his queen away with Qf1+ Rxf1. Qd5 let a won game slip: Qxa3, and after Qxd4, Qxh3 stripped your king — nearly fifteen pawns of advantage gone.
drills.title: vs yassine3453 (860) — Englund Gambit

Qd5 looks natural, centralizing the queen, but it does nothing about that free rook and instead gives Black's queen on b2 time to go hunting: Qxa3, Qxd4, Qxh3 strip your pawns one after another while your rook on e7 gets pushed back to e3 just to survive. When you're this far ahead, the question isn't 'what's a good move' but 'what wins material or ends the game right now' - a hanging piece always answers that first.

drills.explanation: The g5 pawn was attacking your bishop on f4, and Nxg5 meets that head-on — the knight is covered by that same bishop, and after fxg5 Bxg5 Black's kingside pawns are stripped while his pieces retreat to passive squares like Nf6 and Nb8 as Qf3 builds pressure. Bf5+ dropped a whole piece instead: e6 blocked the check and hit the bishop, and after Bc2, gxf4 won your dark-squared bishop.

drills.coachNote: Your bishop on f4 is hanging right now — the pawn on g5 attacks it, and nothing defends it. Instead of fixing that you throw in Bf5+, but Black just answers e6, kicking the checking bishop back to c2, and then plays gxf4 anyway, pocketing the piece you never dealt with — the check bought you nothing but a tempo loss. The move was Nxg5, capturing the attacker first: after fxg5 Bxg5 you're up activity and Black's kingside pawns are wrecked, with Nf6 Qf3 keeping the initiative. Before you hand out a 'free' check, scan for what's already hanging — a check doesn't erase a threat, it just delays it.

drills.explanation: Nxg5 was the shot: after fxg5 Bxg5 you get two pawns for the knight and Black's king on d7 is stranded, with Qf3 coming to hit the loose d5 pawn (the simple e4 was strong too). Bf5+ backfired — e6 blocked with tempo, the bishop crawled back to c2, and gxf4 scooped up your dark-squared bishop, which the g5 pawn had been eyeing all along.

drills.title: vs jatin221272 (817) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Notice Black's king is stuck on d7, wide open in the center — that's what you should be attacking, not chasing a random check. The move was e4: if Black grabs the bishop with gxf4, you answer exd5, hitting the knight on c6, and once it retreats to a7 you get Qa4+, forking the king on d7 along the a4-d7 diagonal — worth far more than the bishop. Instead you played Bf5+ right away, and after e6 Bc2 gxf4 you've simply lost the bishop for nothing, no open lines, no attack. When the enemy king is stuck in the center, look for the pawn break that rips it open before you spend your tactics.

drills.explanation: Your knight on e4 was attacked by the d3 pawn, and Nd6 is the safe retreat — White wins the e5 pawn with Rxe5+, but Be7 blocks, Bg6 follows, and you're only down a pawn with pieces coming out. Ng5 ran the knight straight onto the c1-bishop's diagonal: Bxg5 won it outright, and White grabbed e5 with the knight as well.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: Your knight on e4 is already under fire from the pawn on d3, so the job is finding it a safe square — g5 isn't one, since White's bishop on c1 has a wide-open diagonal through d2-e3-f4 straight to g5. That's why Bxg5 just wins the piece outright, and after f6 Nxe5 Be6 you're down a piece with White's knight raking your position too. The move was Nd6, tucking the knight where nothing attacks it — after Rxe5+ Be7 Qe2 Bg6 you're only down a pawn and still in the fight. Before moving an attacked piece, make sure the new square isn't just trading one attacker for another.

drills.explanation: Your knight on g5 was attacked by the bishop on c1, defended only by your queen along the d8–g5 diagonal — and Be7 blocked that exact diagonal. Bxg5 won the knight, and after Be6, Bxe7 Qxe7 left White a clean piece up. Ne6 just steps to safety; after Qf3 Qf6 Nxc6 Bxd3 the position stays a fair fight.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: Your knight on g5 is still hanging to that same bishop on c1 down the open diagonal, and nothing you've done addresses it. Be7 ignores the threat entirely, so White just plays Bxg5, and after Be6 Bxe7 Qxe7 you've lost the knight for nothing. The move was Ne6, pulling the knight itself out of danger while eyeing the center — after Qf3 Qf6 Nxc6 Bxd3 Qd5 it's still a fight, but you're not just shedding material. When a piece is hanging, the fix has to involve that piece — moving something else doesn't make the threat disappear.

drills.explanation: Bc7 hits the queen on d8 and grabs a square deep in Black's camp: after Qd7, b6 locks the bishop on c7 permanently, cramping the whole queenside while Ra4 swings the rook toward the action. Your e4 gave Black a free move for Bd7, developing with a hit on the b5 pawn — the same Bc7 idea then came a tempo late, and the queen slipped away to c8.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Your bishop on f4 has a clean shot at the queen on d8 — the diagonal f4-e5-d6-c7 is wide open, so Bc7 wins a tempo on the queen for free. After Qd7, b6 clamps down and Nc6 forks the queen and the rook on a8 — that's the real point, a fork two moves down the road, not just a tempo gain. Instead you played e4, and Black gets time for Bd7, tucking the bishop away and defusing the whole idea before you get to it. Before pushing pawns, scan your bishop's diagonal for a piece it's already hitting — here it was pointed straight at the queen.

drills.explanation: Qc5 does three jobs: it confronts the queen on b6, attacks the knight on e7, and keeps the b5 pawn defended. After Qd8, Bd6 piles onto e7, and Bxe7 Rxe7 leaves you in full control of the dark squares. Qc3 left b5 with no defender at all — Bd7 came immediately, and after your too-late Qc5, Bxb5 took the pawn for free.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Your pawn on b5 is attacked by Black's queen on b6, and Qc3 does nothing about it — you just slide sideways while the real problem stays on the board. Sure enough, after Bd7 the pawn falls to Bxb5, handing back material you were up. The move was Qc5, meeting the queen head-on — it forces Qd8 or a trade, and then Bd6 goes after the knight on e7 directly, so if Re8 defends, Bxe7 Rxe7 just wins the piece anyway. When a pawn's attacked, don't play a move that ignores it — either defend it, trade it off, or create a bigger threat that outweighs the loss.

drills.explanation: Nf5+ is a fork: it checks the king on g3 and attacks the rook on g7 at the same time. After Kf4 you play Nxg7, winning the rook and flipping the game — roughly twelve pawns of swing. Nb7 instead walked into Rc7+, and after Kd8 the rook simply captured the knight on b7.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs OdisseoAP (826) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: You're completely winning here, and there's a shot on the board: Nf5+ forks the king on g3 and the rook on g7 — after Kf4 you just play Nxg7 and the rook's yours, with Nh5 and the c-pawn running afterward sealing it. Instead you played Nb7, which threatens nothing, and White's rook swings to c7 with check — Kd8 is forced, then Rxb7 scoops up your own knight for free, the exact fork you should've played, now used against you. That one move swings a completely winning game toward a loss. When you're up material, hunt for your own forks and checks before drifting into a quiet move.

drills.explanation: Bxg3+ wins a pawn with check, and after the forced Kxg3, Rxd1 scoops the rook — d1 had no defender at all, so you net rook and pawn for the bishop. Rd7 put your rook on a square nothing defends (the knight on c6 doesn't cover d7): Rxd7 took it for free, and after Bd6, bxc6 grabbed your knight as well.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs OdisseoAP (826) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: You're up a piece and completely winning, and there's a shot right there: Bxg3+! Your bishop takes the pawn on g3 with check on the king stuck on h2 — after Kxg3, the rook on d1 is undefended, so Rxd1 wins it clean, and Be3 Ne7 Bxa7 still leaves you crushing. Instead you played Rd7, putting your rook on the open d-file directly across from White's rook — but it isn't defended, so Rxd7 wins it outright, no recapture at all. White then mops up the loose knight on c6 with bxc6 too. Before sliding onto an open file, check whether the square you're landing on is just as exposed as the one you left.

drills.explanation: Qxb7+ forces checkmate: the queen grabs b7 and checks the king on e7 along the wide-open seventh rank, Black must block with Qc7, and Qxc7 is mate — your knight on f6 covers the escape squares e8 and d7, and the e5 pawn guards the knight. exd4 was a pawn grab with mate on the board; after Bg7 Black started breathing again.

drills.title: vs pisitto999 (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Your queen has a free shot at b7 — the pawn's undefended, and once you take, the king on e7 is trapped on the 7th rank because your knight on f6 smothers d7 and e8. Black's only reply is ...Qc7 blocking, and then Qxc7 is checkmate. Instead you played exd4, just grabbing a pawn, and after Bg7, dxc5, Qc7, Rd7+ you're merely much better instead of already finished — you traded a forced mate for a long middlegame. When the enemy king is boxed in by its own pieces, always look for the check that rips open the back rank before reaching for a quiet recapture.

drills.explanation: Rd7+ is a deflection: the queen on c7 has to capture, and Nxd7 then forks the rook on b8 and the bishop on f8 — you've won queen for rook, with Rd1 coming to support the knight. Nd7 tried the fork without the preparation: Bg7 simply stepped the bishop out, nothing was won, and Rd6 got met by Rbc8. The open d-file was the key — use it with check first.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs pisitto999 (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Look at your rook on d1 and black's queen on c7 — she's the only thing guarding the rook on d8, and she's tied to the d-file to do it. Rd7+ exploits that: the check forces Qxd7, and your knight on f6, which was already eyeing that square, just scoops the queen with Nxd7 — queen for a rook, straight profit. Instead you played Nd7, a quiet regroup, and after Bg7, Rd6, Rbc8, Rad1 you're still winning but nearly four pawns worse off than you should be. When a defender is pinned to one job like that queen was, look for the forcing move that makes her fail at it.

drills.explanation: Your queen on a4 was attacked by the knight on c5 and had to reach safety first — Qa3 does it. The Qh4 attacking idea was right but needed f6 first: after f6 gxf6, Black's own pawn on f6 blocks the e7–h4 diagonal, and only then is Qh4 strong. Played immediately, Qh4 landed right on the e7-queen's diagonal — Qxh4 won your queen on the spot.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (860) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Your queen jumps to h4, but check the diagonal — black's queen sits on e7, and e7-f6-g5-h4 is a clear line with nothing on it. That's not a threat, that's you parking your queen on a square she's already attacking for free; Qxh4 wins your queen outright, no combination needed. You were already down a pawn here, and that one move turned a tough defense into a lost game. Qa3 was the calm answer — tuck the queen off that diagonal — and after Re8, c4, d4, g4, Kh8 you're still fighting a normal, defensible middlegame. Before you move a piece anywhere, check every line the opponent's most active piece already covers.

drills.explanation: Your e5 pawn was attacked by the d6 pawn; exd6 resolves it cleanly, and after cxd6 you develop normally with Nc3 and Nf3, dead level. Pushing e6 instead placed the pawn on a square Black's f7 pawn covers: fxe6 ate it for free, and after Bd3 Nf6 c4 you were simply a pawn down out of the opening.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (860) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Black just dropped a pawn on d6, sitting there for the taking with exd6, and it comes with a bonus — after cxd6 black's structure loosens and you develop smoothly with Nc3 and Nf3. Instead you pushed e6, and that pawn has zero support; black simply plays fxe6 and pockets it for free, no compensation, no attack behind it. You went from a comfortable +2.5 to roughly even in one move by handing back material you'd already won. When a pawn is hanging in front of you, take it — don't push past it and give your opponent a free capture instead.

drills.explanation: Your queen on e5 was attacked by the knight on f3, and Qe6 was the safe square — it stays active and out of reach, and if Nd4 chases it again, Qe5 returns with White having nothing better than repeating. Qd6 stepped onto the open d-file instead: Rad1 hit the queen with your own rook on d8 lined up behind it, and after Qb4, Rxd8+ Bxd8 handed White the file and the initiative.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (859) — Polish Opening
drills.coachNote: Your queen on e5 is doing real work, pressuring e3 and eyeing h2 alongside your knight on g4 — that's the diagonal you want to stay on. Pulling back to d6 gets off it and hands White the initiative: Rad1 piles down the d-file where your rook on d8 was only being held by that same queen, you're pushed further with Qb4, and Rxd8+ Bxd8 wins White the exchange. Qe6 keeps the queen active on that same diagonal without losing contact with d8, and after Nd4, Qe5, Nf3 nothing's conceded. When your queen is the only thing defending a piece, don't retreat it off-task without checking what you're leaving behind.

drills.explanation: Bxb4 just takes a free pawn — the whole point of testing the Polish. White regains it with Bxe5, but after Nf6, c3, Be7 you've swapped his wing pawn for your e-pawn and developed smoothly. Nc6 guarded e5 but walked into b5: the knight had to retreat to e7, and Bxe5 took the pawn anyway — White kept his extra pawn and gained time.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (859) — Polish Opening
drills.coachNote: White's bishop on b2 is staring straight down at your pawn on e5, and the pawn that just advanced to b4 to open that diagonal is completely undefended — Bxb4 is a free pawn, and it comes with tempo. Instead you played Nc6 to babysit e5, but that doesn't actually fix anything: White plays b5, kicking your knight to the awkward e7 square, and then Bxe5 grabs the pawn anyway once the knight's shoved off. You lose the same pawn a move later and you're worse placed for it. When a pawn's just hanging like that b4 pawn was, take it rather than building a fence around a different one.

drills.explanation: Nd4 does everything at once: it saves the knight from the d5 pawn and attacks White's queen on f3, winning a free tempo. After Qd1 you follow with Bf5 and b5, developing with real energy. Nce7 retreated to a passive square that blocks your own f8 bishop, and gave White time for d4, building a big centre unchallenged.
drills.title: vs Aldr_in (958) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: Your knight on c6 is being harassed by the pawn on d5, sure, but look at what's undefended across the board — White's queen sits on f3 with nothing guarding it from a knight hop to d4. Nd4 hits that queen directly, and after she's forced back with Qd1 you're already developing with tempo via Bf5. Instead you played Nce7, tucking the knight onto a square that blocks in your own bishop on f8 and your queen's diagonal, gaining nothing while White calmly plays d4 and Ne2 and gets comfortable. Before retreating an attacked piece passively, check whether it can jump forward with a threat instead — tempo is currency.

drills.explanation: Kb6 steps to safety, and play stays balanced: Rh5 Rg8, then Rxf5 for him and Rxg3 for you — an even pawn-grab. Kd6 walked onto exactly the square the knight on e5 forks from f7: Nf7+ hits king and rook together, and Ke7 Nxd8 Kxd8 costs you a rook for a knight. From e5, f7 was the springboard covering both d6 and d8.
drills.title: vs Aldr_in (958) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: White's knight on e5 is the piece to watch, because it's one hop from forking two of your pieces at once. Walking the king to d6 lands it on exactly the square Nf7+ forks from: that check hits your king and the rook on d8 in the same move, and after Ke7, Nxd8+, Kxd8 White pockets the exchange for nothing. Kb6 sidesteps the fork entirely, tucking the king toward your queenside pawns instead, and the game stays a real fight — Rh5, Rg8, Rxf5, Rxg3, b4 gives you counterplay to hold with. In knight endgames, always check which of your own pieces share a knight-move with your king before you plant it on a square.

drills.explanation: The e5 pawn was attacking your bishop on f4, and Nxe5 turns the threat around: it wins the pawn, and after Nxe5 Bxe5 your bishop sits beautifully in the center eyeing g7, leaving Black scrambling with Qg6 before you castle and meet Bf5 calmly. Castling first simply dropped the bishop — exf4 took it for free, and you were a piece down by move nine.
drills.title: vs dangalindo97 (884) — London System
drills.coachNote: Your bishop on f4 has zero protection, and Black's pawn on e5 sits right next to it with a clean diagonal shot — pawns capture diagonally, so exf4 was live the instant you played a quiet move instead of addressing it. That's exactly what happened: O-O ignored the threat, exf4 won the bishop for free, and c4, Nf6, Re1+ afterward don't get it back — Black just keeps the extra piece while you scramble for activity. The move was Nxe5: grab the e5 pawn yourself first, before Black's pawn can grab your bishop. After Nxe5 Nxe5 Bxe5, your bishop recaptures safely on e5 instead of dying on f4, eyeing the long diagonal, and you're simply a pawn up with Qg6, O-O, Bf5 flowing naturally next. Before any quiet move, scan what enemy pawns can capture right now.

drills.explanation: Qg4 stepped straight onto the c8-bishop's open diagonal — c8 to g4 had nothing in the way, and Bxg4 took the queen; after h3, Be6 the bishop went home and Black was simply up material. Qh5 was the safe square, or better yet Nd2 first: develop the stranded b1 knight, tuck the queen on e1, and Nf3 finally challenges the bishop on g5.
drills.title: vs dangalindo97 (884) — London System
drills.coachNote: There's a bishop sitting on c8 the whole game, and the diagonal from c8 to h3 is wide open — d7, e6, and f5 are all empty. Qg4 puts your queen right on that diagonal, so Bxg4 just wins it for a bishop, on top of a position where you were already down close to four pawns of material. That's the swing: you weren't just losing, you handed over the queen for nothing, and h3, Be6, Nd2 afterward doesn't change that you're now down a queen with nothing to show for it. Qh5 sits one square further along that same diagonal, completely safe from the bishop, while still eyeing e5 and f4 — you keep fighting with Nd2, Be6, Rxf4 clawing back the f4 pawn instead of handing over material. When a long diagonal is wide open toward your queen, check every square on it before you move there.

drills.explanation: Both Black bishops were loose — f5 to your bishop on d3, g5 to your knight — but capture order decided everything. Bxf5 takes the one with a counter-capture available, since the f5 bishop and your d3 bishop attack each other; after gxf5, Nd4 centralizes powerfully. Nxg5 allowed the in-between move Bxd3, and after Qxd3 Qxg5 Black had won the piece right back.
drills.title: vs LeoAlayon (759) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Black's bishop on f5 is the piece demanding your attention — it's aimed straight at your bishop on d3. Instead of dealing with it, you went pawn-hunting with Nxg5, and Black answers Bxd3, trading into your queen; you recapture Qxd3, but then Qxg5 snaps back the knight you just captured with, and you come out of it a full piece down, on top of a position that was already shaky. Bxf5 deals with the actual threat first: you take the bishop that's attacking you before grabbing anything else, and after gxf5 recaptures, material's even and the position simplifies cleanly toward Nd4, Nxd4, cxd4, h4. The principle: when an enemy piece is attacking one of yours, capture or resolve that first — pawns and other targets can wait.

drills.explanation: Bxf5 resolves the bishop standoff your way: after Bxg5 Nxg5 Qxg5 you have Bd7 — the bishop lands in Black's camp hitting the knight on c6 and the rook on e8. dxe5 handed Black the move order: Bxg5 came first, and after Bxf5 gxf5 Nd4 the trades fizzled — about a pawn and a half lost purely to capturing in the wrong sequence.
drills.title: vs LeoAlayon (759) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: You had a small edge here (+0.6) and grabbed material with dxe5, but that let Black's bishop on f6 swing over and take yours on g5 — Bxg5. You get some back with Bxf5, trading bishops, but after gxf5 recaptures, Black's knight jumps into d4, a monster outpost sitting in the middle of your position, and you come out of the whole sequence worse off. The move was Bxf5 immediately — deal with the tension between your g5 bishop and Black's bishops before you go collect the e5 pawn. Then Bxg5, Nxg5, Qxg5 simplifies in your favor, and Black's best is just quiet moves like Bd7 and Reb8, nothing dangerous. Same lesson as the very next move you played: resolve the piece tension on the kingside before reaching for a pawn elsewhere on the board.

drills.explanation: Your queen on a8 had the bishop on c8 pinned against the queen on d8, and Rfc1 — either rook works, but the f1 rook keeps a1 at home — piles onto it down the fully open c-file. Black's best is to bail out with Be6, when Qxd8+ Nxd8 trades into a pleasant endgame for you. g3 let the moment slip: d5 and then Nd6 covered c8, and the target wriggled free.

drills.title: vs hansk74 (917) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: You're up massively here, +6.3, with your queen deep on a8, but g3 doesn't do anything for you — your rook on f1 is still sitting idle, and it gives Black time to get organized. After g3, Black plays d5 and routes the knight from f7 to d6, and by the time you tuck your king in with Kh1, two pawns of advantage have quietly evaporated just because you handed over tempo. Rfc1 keeps pressing: it activates your last piece, and after Be6, Qxd8+ trades queens exactly when you want to — you're so far ahead that keeping queens on the board is only extra risk, not extra winning chances. Once Nxd8 recaptures, you push d5 yourself, Black's bishop takes on d5, and you're converting cleanly instead of giving your opponent room for complications. When you're winning big, look for the move that activates your last piece or forces simplification, not a slow luft move that just passes the turn.

drills.explanation: Nxe4 wins the e4 pawn cleanly — d5 can't recapture, because that would open the b3–g8 diagonal from your queen straight onto Black's king. After f5 the knight slides back to g3, and c4 starts prying at d5 next. Nh2 retreated for nothing: f5 cemented Black's pawn on e4, and you had to play f3 to challenge it anyway, a tempo and a pawn poorer.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs hansk74 (917) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Black's pawn on e4 looks defended by the d5 pawn, but that recapture is a trap, not a real defense — take it with Nxe4, and if dxe4, you've just blown open the diagonal from your queen on b3 all the way to f7, right next to Black's king. That's why the engine line has Black just play f5 instead of recapturing, letting you keep the pawn clean while Ng3 tucks your knight back to safety — you're simply a pawn up heading into g5, c4, Be6. Instead you played Nh2, moving the wrong knight and leaving e4 alone; now f5 props that pawn up for good, and by the time you challenge it with f3, Black's already consolidated with Re8. The pawn stays a permanent thorn instead of disappearing. The lesson: before assuming an advanced pawn is defended, check what recapturing there actually costs the defender.
